children: By Mike Scarcella

In a span of three days this month, a defense lawyer was rebuked for filing fabricated police witness testimony in a New Mexico murder case, prosecutors in Oklahoma disclosed that a judge's order there had cited fake cases, and a lawyer representing State Farm in Los Angeles was fined for erroneous citations across seven court filings.

The materials in each case were produced using generative AI, adding to a mountain of made-up, misquoted, misleading or incorrectly cited legal filings since the technology debuted on a mass scale in 2022.

Three years after the first US court sanction over AI-generated errors, the number of attorneys admitting they used AI carelessly keeps growing, with AI errors now seeping into court opinions, expert testimony and prosecutors' briefs.

"You would have thought that the legal profession — armed with awareness that hallucinations can happen — would be more vigilant," said US District Judge P. Kevin Castel in Manhattan, whose 2023 order sanctioning lawyers for citing fake ChatGPT-generated cases became the profession's earliest warning.

Castel told Reuters that scrutiny from judges and the adversarial legal system meant AI errors were being exposed when they occur, and "that’s a wonderful thing.” But "as the problem continues without abatement, the need for sanctions that are a greater deterrent grows," he said.

AI "hallucinations" have now surfaced in at least 1,395 cases in US state and federal courts, according to a researcher tracking the cases on his website. Lawyers are generally not prohibited from using AI, but they are bound by ethics rules to verify the accuracy of their court submissions.

After a lawyer in New Mexico cited fabricated witnesses and made-up police testimony in his client's murder appeal, justices on the state's Supreme Court at a hearing last month expressed exasperation that attorneys were still failing to vet their AI research.
“My 13-year-old nephew knows about hallucinations,” Justice C. Shannon Bacon had told the defense lawyer. “My 75-year-old stepmother knows about hallucinations.”

Bacon said the lawyer either chose not to understand the technology's limitations or "decided to roll the dice." The lawyer in that case told Reuters he was remorseful and called the incident "a lesson learned for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology."

Mark McKenna, co-director of the UCLA Institute of Technology, Law & Policy, blamed a mix of factors as contributing to the growing number of errors: a competitive rush among law firms to adopt AI, pressure to deliver work quickly and AI marketing that he said downplays risks.
“Lawyers keep making the judgment that the upside is better than the downside,” McKenna said.

The sanctions lawyers that have faced range from warnings and formal rebukes to monetary penalties in the hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars. Some judges have referred lawyers to state bar authorities to consider their compliance with professional ethics rules.
In California last week, a lawyer representing State Farm was fined $999.99 after generative AI produced a series of inaccurate citations and quotations.
"I accept full responsibility for my erroneous citations and make no excuses and express my deepest and sincerest apologies to the court," the lawyer had told the court.

State Farm in a statement this week said it “expects all external counsel to adhere to the highest standards of professionalism ​and ethical conduct, including ​when using AI and when reviewing and confirming the accuracy of all court filings.”

AI errors in judicial rulings have been rarer but have raised particular alarms. After hallucinated material was included in decisions by two federal judges last year, US Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa called on judges across the country to "formalize measures to prevent the misuse of artificial intelligence in their chambers."
In the Oklahoma case last week, a judge told a state investigator he had used an AI program for research and that an order he drafted contained two citations to non-existent cases.
A lawyer for the judge said they were declining to comment.
